title: National Parks and Sanctuaries in the News

cards.b:
UPSC often builds questions from a park in the news: where it is, what it holds, what the issue is. A static fact (state, species, legal category) plus a news hook is the pattern.

This lesson gives the legal base and then recent cases. Check the latest figures as they change, and treat counts as "as of" values.

Under the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972: sanctuaries are declared under Section 26A (earlier Section 18) and allow some activities like grazing with permission. National parks are declared under Section 35, with stricter bans on grazing and private rights. Conservation reserves (Section 36A) and community reserves (Section 36C) cover government and community land. Tiger reserves come under Section 38V.

India has over 100 national parks and over 500 sanctuaries, covering about 5 percent of land (counts as of recent years).

The Great Nicobar Island project (about Rs 72,000 crore, with a transshipment port, airport, township and power plant) is a repeated news item. It needs diversion of about 130 sq km of forest and sits near Campbell Bay National Park and the Great Nicobar Biosphere Reserve. The area is home to the Shompen, a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group, and the Nicobar megapode. The Galathea Bay Wildlife Sanctuary was denotified in 2021 for the port. NGT and Calcutta High Court reviews and Forest Rights Act concerns have been raised.

The Ken-Betwa Link Project (agreement in 2021, foundation in December 2024) will divert water from the Ken to the Betwa in Bundelkhand. Part of the Panna Tiger Reserve (Madhya Pradesh) will be submerged, with about a tenth of its area affected as per reports. The reserve is also a UNESCO biosphere reserve (2020). The Supreme Court's Central Empowered Committee flagged the tiger habitat loss. Compensation plans include a new tiger landscape.

Kaziranga (Assam) holds two-thirds of the world's one-horned rhinos. Floods push animals onto NH-715, so an elevated corridor was approved in 2025 (check the status). Gir (Gujarat) is the only home of the Asiatic lion. The census showed about 674 lions in 2020 and a higher count reported in 2025 (about 891, to be verified). Lions now live outside the park in the Saurashtra region, and Barda sanctuary is seen as a second home. Kuno is a past plan for a second lion site.

Kuno National Park (Madhya Pradesh) hosts the cheetah project. Bandipur and Nagarhole are the site of the night-traffic ban on NH-766 (Kerala demand versus Supreme Court). Jim Corbett drew a Supreme Court rebuke in 2024 over tree felling and illegal construction for a tiger safari at Pakhrau. Sariska and Ranthambore saw tiger translocations. The Ratapani sanctuary in Madhya Pradesh was notified as a tiger reserve in recent years.

Governments say strategic roads, ports and irrigation matter. Conservationists say forest diversion damages the very sites they claim to protect. Compensatory afforestation does not recreate old forest. The Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act 2023 has been challenged on the same grounds.

A useful frame: avoid, minimise, then compensate. Ask whether the project truly needs this site.

For each park in the news, note five things: state, legal category, key species, the issue and the law or body involved (NTCA, NBWL, Forest Rights Act, CAMPA). Create a one-line summary. Use the latest Hindu or Indian Express report for numbers, and mark them with the year.

• Sanctuary: Section 26A. National Park: Section 35. Tiger reserve: 38V.
  • Kaziranga: Assam, rhino. Gir: lion. Kuno: cheetah. Panna: Ken-Betwa.
  • Great Nicobar: Campbell Bay NP, Shompen.
  • Check each year's newest additions.

Keep a notebook page with one line per park: state, category, species, issue. Mark each fact with its year.

Prelims-style: "Consider the following protected areas and their states." "Which of these is a tiger reserve?" Know pairs like Panna-Madhya Pradesh and Pakke-Arunachal.

Mains-style: "Infrastructure projects near protected areas pose a dilemma. Discuss with examples." Structure: legal safeguards; Ken-Betwa and Great Nicobar; court and NBWL role; compensation limits; way forward.
